Only two studies directly compared mandatory and voluntary policies, with one favoring the intervention (though not significantly), and no studies examined different stages of policy implementation. Regarding policies aimed at restricting food marketing to children: Studies targeting children over 12 years old (3 out of 4 studies) were more likely to favor the intervention compared to those targeting children 12 years old or younger (1 out of 12 studies). Policies restricting the use of promotional characters (3 out of 10 studies) were more effective than those addressing broader child-appealing techniques (1 out of 5 studies) or animation techniques (0 out of 1 study). Television food advertising (3 out of 10 studies) demonstrated more impact compared to digital media marketing (0 out of 3 studies) or product packaging (1 out of 3 studies). In terms of purchasing behavior, five observational studies suggested that food marketing policies may reduce food purchasing, with significant decreases reported in some cases. However, no studies reported outcomes related to food choice, dietary intake, food preferences, body weight, or obesity. Evidence on dietary intake and product changes was very uncertain, with limited data available. The review also highlighted that unintended consequences of food marketing policies could sometimes benefit public health. For example, some studies reported reduced unhealthy food volumes in households and lower prices for children’s breakfast cereals in jurisdictions with mandatory policies. The quality of evidence varied, with some studies being of high quality and clearly favoring interventions, while others were of moderate quality or showed mixed results. Subgroup analyses were not feasible for certain outcomes due to insufficient data. Declarations of interest from contributors to the guideline development process were assessed, and none were deemed to pose a conflict of interest. This included funding from various organizations, participation in advisory roles, and involvement in research or policy-related activities. All engagements were evaluated in the context of the guideline's focus, and no risks to the guideline development process were identified.
